planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost on the soil surface under light; transplant divisions or seedlings after frost once soil has warmed.

directions: This central/eastern European wild thyme forms a loose, slightly fuzzy gray-green mat topped with lilac-pink flower spikes in summer, and is noticeably more cold- and drought-tolerant than creeping thyme cultivars. Plant in lean, fast-draining soil and avoid rich amendments, which encourage rot and floppy growth. Use as a dry-slope or rock-garden groundcover rather than a foot-traffic path plant, since its habit is looser than Thymus serpyllum. Shear back lightly after bloom to keep the mat dense.

planting.note: Best established from rooted cuttings or divisions set out after last frost; seed is rarely offered and germination is slow and uneven.

directions: Native to Mediterranean coastal cliffs, this thyme forms an exceptionally flat, glossy dark-green mat prized as a between-pavers or lawn-substitute groundcover in mild climates. It is less frost-hardy than Thymus serpyllum and needs reliably sharp drainage plus protection from winter wet. Mow or shear only lightly, since the species naturally stays under 3 inches tall. Light foot traffic releases a strong lemon-thyme fragrance.

planting.note: Propagate by cuttings and set out after last frost; this species is grown almost exclusively from vegetative starts by specialty nurseries rather than seed.

directions: Endemic to coastal Portugal, this thyme has woolly gray-green leaves with a strong camphor scent and pale lilac flowers, and is grown by rock-garden specialists as a parent of several hardy hybrid thymes. Give it gritty, lime-rich, very sharply drained soil and full sun, and protect from prolonged winter wet rather than cold alone. It resents heavy clay and overhead irrigation. Trim lightly after flowering to maintain a compact mound.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant or move containers outdoors once nights stay above freezing.

directions: This Greek species is the straight species behind the popular ornamental hybrids 'Kent Beauty' and 'Barbara Tingey', producing trailing stems of rounded gray-green leaves and papery, hop-like chartreuse-pink bracts in summer. It is grown chiefly as an ornamental for rock gardens, walls, and hanging containers rather than for cooking. Plant in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil and avoid winter wet, which it tolerates poorly in cold climates; treat as a container plant and overwinter indoors where not reliably hardy. Deadhead spent flower bracts to extend bloom.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors or into containers after danger of frost has passed.

directions: Endemic to Crete, this diminutive oregano has tiny, intensely pungent leaves on a compact mounding plant well suited to herb pots, troughs, and edging. It needs the same lean, fast-draining soil and full sun as other Mediterranean oreganos, and resents rich or waterlogged ground. In colder zones grow it in a container that can be moved under cover for winter. Snip sprigs regularly to encourage bushy new growth and prevent legginess.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant or set out containers after last frost once soil has warmed.

directions: This Greek rock-garden oregano is grown for its distinctive spurred, purplish-pink calyces held above low mats of small gray-green leaves, giving a similar ornamental effect to Origanum rotundifolium. Grow in gritty, neutral-to-alkaline, very sharply drained soil in full sun, and keep dry in winter. It suits raised beds, troughs, and rock gardens where its small scale will not be overwhelmed by neighbors. Trim back after flowering to keep the mat tight.
